title: Checkout payments
brief: Online shops send you their customers at the moment they pay. You call a card processor, record the order and answer in a couple of seconds. When the processor is slow or down, shoppers refresh and tap Pay again.

clarify.q: What happens if the shopper taps Pay twice?
clarify.a: They must be charged once. Every attempt carries a unique key from the browser.

clarify.q: If the processor is down, should checkout fail?
clarify.a: Better to say "payment pending" and settle after than to lose the sale, as long as nobody is charged twice.
Yes. Payments need an audit trail and keys held in a key service.
About 0.4 s typically and 2 s at the slow end. It accepts about 1,000 charges a second for you.

notes: The processor itself is paid from revenue and is not in this budget.

numbers.label: Servers tied up waiting for a 2 s processor
Order records written per day at 55 percent average load

hints: When the processor is slow, your servers wait on it and run out of room for everyone else. How do you stop waiting?
Two ideas fit: a circuit breaker that fails fast when the processor is sick, or a queue that accepts the payment now and settles later. An idempotency key makes retries safe either way.
State transitions and event publication must be atomic and monotonic. Measure the failed boundary, waiting time and retry work before choosing a change.

editorial.summary: A checkout is mostly a chain of waits, and the processor is the slowest link. Two patterns are common, and only one survives this day. The asynchronous one accepts the payment into a queue, answers "pending" at once and lets workers settle with the processor at its own pace, which rides out the full processor outage. The synchronous one keeps the shopper on the line and protects your servers with a short timeout, a circuit breaker and idempotency keys, but while the processor is down nobody can pay.

designs.name: Accept now, settle after
designs.why: Payments go into a queue and the shopper sees "payment pending". Workers settle with the processor, retrying later if it is down. Nothing is lost during an outage, and the checkout pages never wait on the processor.

designs.name: Pending payments with read replicas
designs.why: A queue accepts payments while the provider is slow or unavailable. Workers use stable provider keys to reconcile unknown outcomes. Read replicas serve browsing while payment recovery continues.

tradeoffs: Synchronous is simpler and gives instant "paid" or "declined". Its weak spot is a full outage: while the processor is down, nobody can pay.
Asynchronous survives an outage and smooths bursts, but the shopper has to accept "pending", and your support team has to explain it.
A circuit breaker trades a few failed payments for keeping the whole checkout alive. Without it, every server ends up waiting on one sick dependency.
The idempotency store adds about 2 ms per payment and prevents the double charge. It is the cheapest insurance in the design.
Timeouts of 30 seconds, the default, feel safe and are the most dangerous setting: a slow processor then ties up every server.
editorial.realWorld: Large checkout providers answer a card charge in about 1 to 2 seconds at the 99th percentile and require an idempotency key on every charge request (approx.).

correctness.prompt: The payment provider times out after accepting a charge. What idempotency key and payment state transitions would make a second tap safe?
correctness.discussion: Use a stable key for the logical payment, not a new key for each attempt, and bind it to the payer, amount and currency. Enforce uniqueness and store pending, succeeded and failed states durably. A timeout leaves the outcome unknown, so reconcile with the provider using the same key rather than start a fresh charge. Apply callbacks conditionally so a late failure cannot overwrite success. Record the order update and its outbox event together; a cache lookup followed by a charge leaves a race. A missing reply does not prove the provider rejected payment. Provider idempotency or status reconciliation is needed for one external effect. State transitions and event publication must be atomic and monotonic.

fields.label: Step 1. Charge P times out. Is it failed?
options: Keep P pending with an unknown outcome
Declare failure and start a new charge
fields.explanation: A missing reply does not prove the provider rejected payment.

fields.label: Step 2. The buyer taps Pay again. Which key is sent?
options: The same logical payment key bound to amount and currency
A fresh key for a faster retry
fields.explanation: Provider idempotency or status reconciliation is needed for one external effect.

fields.label: Step 3. Success callback arrives twice, then an old failure arrives. What commits?
options: One conditional terminal success plus an order outbox; ignore stale regression
fields.explanation: State transitions and event publication must be atomic and monotonic.

correctness.responsibility: Resolve unknown charges and keep order state consistent with payment state.
correctness.limits: The traffic model does not execute this protocol. The checked trace covers its central responsibility; the written explanation is retained for review.

twist.brief: Demand has settled at about 500 requests/s. The new monthly ceiling is $2458. The original burst reserve now competes with the operating budget. Decide which reserve to keep, then test its failure headroom. All data and recovery promises still apply.

design.name: Smaller workload, measured reserve
design.why: Reduce the paid floor for the quieter workload, preserving the required copies and recovery settings. This design was checked through the full event day.
